newsitem.title: FRANCE: Weather threatens French grain yields -crop expert.
newsitem.headline: Weather threatens French grain yields -crop expert.

text.p: Persistent dry and cold weather has already done some serious damage in France and experts now predict possible yield losses of 10 to 20 percent for winter grains.
Rain is expected in France over the weekend but it may come too late to significantly limit the damage, a crop expert for the French ACPA farm lobby told Reuters.
"If there was substantial rain today across France, this could change certain things. But in any case, some of the damage cannot be limited," ACPA expert Jean-Noel Terrible said.
"In any case yields will be hit," he added.
The average grain yield was 7.1 tonnes per hectare in 1996 and total grain production reached 62.46 million tonnes.
Winter crops, particularly durum wheat, have been the hardest hit by a combination of dry weather and nightly frost.
In the main production areas of southern France experts already predict losses of up to 40 percent for durum wheat yields.
Across France winter durum wheat yield could fall by some 25 percent, Terrible predicted.
At end-March crop experts were still cautious, hoping crops would recover if there was a break in the weather.
But today there are growing fears that farmers may be heading for a "disaster" after a three-month dry spell, Terrible said.
Ironically substantial rains, if they materialise, may not prove that beneficial as it could wash away from the soil the nitrogen that is crucial to crop development, the expert said.
The three-month dry spell is also threatening to disrupt spring sowings.
Maize sowings have started in northern France but dry soils are delaying operations in the south.
Some farmers, concerned over possible irrigation curbs, may also decide to plant more drought-resistant sunflower or sorghum and less maize, experts said.
